title: Pentecost (Acts 2:1–13)
hookLine: wind, flames, and every visitor hears the good news in their own language

cards: A street market in a big city on a holiday weekend: every stall shouting, a grandmother bargaining in one language, a kid answering in another. That's Jerusalem on the morning of this story.
It's a Jewish festival, and pilgrims have come from all over the known world. Acts lists them: Parthians and Medes, people from Mesopotamia, Egypt and Libya, Cretes, Arabians and visitors from Rome.
Meanwhile about a hundred and twenty followers of Jesus wait together in one house, as they were told to. Then, Acts says, a noise from the sky like a violent wind fills the whole house.
A crowd comes running, and what they hear next makes no sense at all.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." Flames, resting on each person. And they begin to speak in other languages.

The crowd hears Galileans, country people from up north, speaking their own mother tongues: "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" Some are amazed. Some sneer that they're full of new wine.
Peter stands up: they're not drunk, it's nine in the morning.

Pentecost is Greek for the fiftieth day. Jews had long counted fifty days from Passover to the Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, a harvest festival that many Jews also came to link with the giving of the law at Sinai.
The miracle: nobody is made to speak one language; everyone hears in their own.
The good news doesn't ask the crowd to cross over to it; it crosses over to them. Many Christians read this as the undoing of Babel, the old story where one language was scattered into many.
Here the many languages stay, and understanding comes anyway.
Christians call Pentecost the birthday of the church, understand it as the coming of the Holy Spirit, and keep it fifty days after Easter, often in red, the color of flame.
Pentecostal churches take their name from this day, and many pray in tongues; other churches see the gift as belonging mainly to the early church, or as rare.
All of them keep the picture: every language.

how: Christians celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter as the coming of the Holy Spirit and the birthday of the church. Many churches decorate in red, read Acts 2, and sometimes read it aloud in several languages at once.

o: the fiftieth day, when the Spirit came in flame
a Greek word for the gift of speaking in tongues
a Latin name for the bishop's tall hat

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: cloven tongues like as of fire

s: at Pentecost everyone was made to speak one language
each visitor heard in his own tongue. the many languages stayed.
Pentecost was already a festival before this story
it was the Jewish Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover. that's why Jerusalem was full of pilgrims.
Peter says they're not drunk because it's too early
it was only nine in the morning, the third hour of the day.

games.q: you're a pilgrim from far away, in Jerusalem for the festival. you hear a roar like wind, and then Galileans speaking your own mother tongue. what do you do?
o: walk on. it's just more festival noise.
stop, amazed, and ask what this means.
games.why: most are amazed and ask, what meaneth this? some mock that they're full of new wine. Peter stands up and answers them.

practice: Picture someone you'll see this week whose language isn't yours, a first language or a grandparent's slang, a teenager's, a coworker's jargon, and ask how they'd say hello.
If you know the words, say them quietly until they feel less strange in your mouth; if not, make a note to ask. If you pray, hold that person before God, in whatever language comes.

wordCard.voice: Pentecost. Greek for the fiftieth day: the Jewish Feast of Weeks, and for Christians the day the Spirit came, in flame and every tongue.

orig.note: Greek: the fiftieth (day), fifty days from Passover; Greek-speaking Jews used it for the Feast of Weeks.

carryVoice: Your line: every language. Tomorrow, the first community shares what it owns. That's seventy-five days in.
